title: Checklist: Your Rights and Dealing With Police
summary: All your constitutional rights and police-related rights, in the simplest words.

body.text: This is the first part of your complete rights checklist. Read one point at a time. You do not have to remember the law's name - just know what you can do.
Part 1: Your basic rights (from the Constitution)

items: 1. Everyone is equal before the law. The government cannot treat you unfairly for no reason. (Article 14)
2. No discrimination. The government cannot treat you badly because of your religion, race, caste, sex or birthplace. (Article 15)
3. Equal chance in government jobs. Everyone gets a fair chance; reserved posts are allowed by the Constitution. (Article 16)
4. Freedom of speech. You can speak and write freely - but not to threaten, spread hate or defame anyone. (Article 19(1)(a))
5. Freedom to gather peacefully. You can hold peaceful meetings and processions, with reasonable limits. (Article 19(1)(b))
6. Freedom to form groups. You can join or start unions, clubs and associations. (Article 19(1)(c))
7. Freedom to move around. You can travel anywhere in India. (Article 19(1)(d))
8. Freedom to settle anywhere. You can choose where to live in India. (Article 19(1)(e))
9. Freedom to do business. You can choose any lawful job, trade or business. (Article 19(1)(g))
10. Right to life and personal liberty. You have a right to live with dignity, privacy and safety. (Article 21)
11. Right to education. Every child aged 6 to 14 has a right to free and compulsory education. (Article 21A)

12. Protection in criminal cases. You cannot be punished for something that was not a crime when it happened; you cannot be punished twice for the same offence; you cannot be forced to confess. (Article 20)
13. Protection when arrested. You must be told why, allowed a lawyer, and taken to a judge within 24 hours. (Article 22)
14. Freedom of religion. You can follow, practise and peacefully spread your religion. (Articles 25-28)
15. Cultural and educational rights. Minority groups can protect their language, culture and their own schools. (Articles 29-30)
16. Right to go to court. If any right is broken, you can go to the Supreme Court (Article 32) or a High Court (Article 226).
17. No human trafficking or forced labour. Nobody can make you work by force or traffic you. (Article 23)
18. No child labour. Children below 14 cannot work in factories, mines or other hazardous jobs. (Article 24)

body.text: Most of these rights are for every person living in India. A few, like Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29, are only for citizens.

items: 19. FIR. This is the written report of a serious (cognisable) crime, recorded at the police station. You can get a free copy.
20. Zero FIR. You can report a serious crime at ANY police station, even one outside its area. They must record it and pass it on.
21. Complaint, FIR and case. A complaint is the information you give; an FIR is the formal record; a case is what a court decides.
22. Arrest without warrant. Police can arrest without a warrant only in the situations the law allows - not just because of any allegation.
23. Grounds of arrest. You have a right to be told why you are being arrested.
24. Right to a lawyer. You can call and be defended by a lawyer of your choice.
25. 24-hour rule. You must be produced before a judge within 24 hours of arrest (leaving out travel time).
26. Bail. In a bailable offence you can be released on bail as a right. In a non-bailable offence, the court decides.
27. No self-incrimination. You cannot be forced to be a witness against yourself. (Article 20(3))
28. Innocent until proven guilty. You are presumed innocent until the court finds you guilty.
29. Free legal aid. If you cannot afford a lawyer, you can get free legal help. Call 15100.
30. Search and seizure. Police must follow the legal procedure. You can ask for the reason and for independent witnesses.
31. Summons and notices. Never ignore a lawful notice or court summons. Find out what it means and what you must do.
32. Witness rights and duties. A witness must tell the truth, and is protected from being intimidated.
33. Private defence. You may defend yourself or another person from an attack, but only as much force as is truly needed.
34. Defamation. False statements that damage someone's reputation can have legal consequences. Honest criticism is allowed.
35. Assault, threats and stalking. Physical violence, intimidation and stalking are offences.
36. Digital evidence. Save original messages, call records and receipts. Never alter or fake evidence.

body.text: From 1 July 2024, new criminal laws replaced the old ones: BNS (offences), BNSS (procedure, arrest, bail) and BSA (evidence).
Never sign anything you have not read, and never pay money to 'settle' a police matter informally. Get everything in writing.

practicalSteps: Save 112 (emergency) and 15100 (free legal aid) on your phone.
If arrested, ask for the reason, tell a family member, and ask for a lawyer.
Always keep a copy of any FIR, notice or complaint you file.
If police refuse to register your FIR, go to the Superintendent of Police or the Magistrate.
exceptions: Fundamental Rights are not all absolute. Reasonable restrictions apply, and some rights are only for citizens.
Some special laws (like preventive detention) allow detention without a normal charge, but with safeguards.

faqs.q: Do I need to know the law's name to use my right?
faqs.a: No. Knowing what you can do is enough. The section numbers are only to help you or your lawyer look it up.

faqs.q: What if I cannot afford a lawyer?
faqs.a: Free legal aid is available for those who qualify. Call the NALSA helpline 15100 or visit your District Legal Services Authority.

misconceptions.myth: The police can keep me as long as they want before a court hearing.
misconceptions.fact: No. You must be produced before a judge within 24 hours of arrest.
